questions.text: A classifier trained on fraud_flag (3% positive) predicts 'no fraud' for every record. Its accuracy is 97%. Its recall on fraud is:
questions.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN). If the model never predicts fraud, TP = 0, so recall = 0/(0 + all frauds) = 0%. The 97% accuracy is entirely from correctly labelling non-fraud records.

questions.text: SMOTE generates synthetic minority samples by:
options: Interpolating between a minority record and one of its k nearest minority neighbours
Removing the majority class records that are furthest from the decision boundary
questions.explanation: SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) creates new synthetic minority samples by interpolating between an existing minority record and one of its k nearest minority neighbours. This produces more diverse synthetic examples than simple duplication.

questions.text: SMOTE oversampling should be applied to the entire dataset (train + test) before splitting.
questions.explanation: SMOTE must be applied ONLY to the training set, after the train-test split. Applying it before the split would allow synthetic training points to be created from test observations, causing data leakage and inflated performance estimates.

questions.text: Why is AUC-PR (Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve) preferred over AUC-ROC for rare event detection?
options: AUC-PR is always larger than AUC-ROC
AUC-ROC can look optimistic when the negative class is very large; AUC-PR focuses on the minority class performance
AUC-PR does not require a threshold to compute
AUC-ROC only works for binary classifiers
questions.explanation: AUC-ROC is affected by a large number of true negatives (which are easy to classify). With 97% negatives, a naïve classifier can achieve high AUC-ROC. AUC-PR focuses entirely on the precision and recall of the minority class, making it a better diagnostic for rare events.

questions.text: Lowering the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.2 will generally:
questions.explanation: Lowering the threshold means more records are predicted positive — catching more actual positives (higher recall) but also more false positives (lower precision). The optimal threshold depends on the business cost of false negatives vs false positives.
